body:
The Information Technology Act, 2000

The Information Technology Act, 2000 is India's principal foundational legislation for legal recognition of electronic records and transactions and for addressing specified computer-related offences. It is Act 21 of 2000, enacted on 9 June 2000, and its principal provisions came into force on 17 October 2000.

The Act connects the legal use of electronic information with rules concerning unauthorised computer-related acts, electronic identity misuse and cyber incident response. For prelims, the most useful task is to distinguish the purposes of selected provisions rather than memorising every section.

Important provisions of the IT Act

SectionMain subjectPrelims distinction
4Legal recognition of electronic records.Relates to the legal status of information in electronic form.
5Legal recognition of electronic signatures.Relates to electronic authentication of records.
43Compensation for specified unauthorised acts involving computer resources, including access or damage.Concerns civil liability for acts covered by the provision.
66Computer-related offences involving acts referred to in Section 43, such as unauthorised access to or damage to computer resources, when committed dishonestly or fraudulently.The dishonest or fraudulent element is significant.
66CIdentity theft involving fraudulent or dishonest use of another person's electronic signature, password or unique identification feature.Focuses on misuse of another person's electronic identity.
66DCheating by personation using a computer resource or communication device.Focuses on cheating while impersonating someone through digital means.
70BIndian Computer Emergency Response Team.Provides the statutory basis for the national cyber incident response agency.

Identity theft versus cheating by personation

Section 66C concerns fraudulent or dishonest use of another person's electronic identity-related credential, such as a password or unique identification feature. Section 66D concerns cheating by pretending to be another person through a computer resource or communication device.

For example, dishonest use of another person's password directly illustrates the subject of Section 66C. A criminal who pretends to be a bank officer during a fraudulent digital interaction to cheat a customer illustrates the type of conduct addressed by Section 66D. A real incident may involve more than one provision, depending on its facts.

Section 66A is not an enforceable cybercrime provision. The Supreme Court struck it down in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India on 24 March 2015. It is shown as omitted in the updated text of the IT Act. Do not confuse Section 66A with Section 66, Section 66C or Section 66D.

CERT-In: India's national cyber incident response agency

CERT-In stands for Indian Computer Emergency Response Team. It operates under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) and serves as the national agency for responding to cybersecurity incidents under Section 70B of the IT Act.

Its functions include collecting and analysing information about cyber incidents, issuing alerts and advisories, recommending preventive measures and coordinating responses to cybersecurity incidents. These functions concern cybersecurity preparedness and technical incident response.

CERT-In should not be confused with a police station or the main public system for registering an individual's financial fraud complaint.

Institutions and public reporting routes

India also has a national arrangement for reporting cybercrime and coordinating action among investigating agencies. The Ministry of Home Affairs established the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) to strengthen coordination in dealing with cybercrime.

Institution or serviceAdministrative connectionMain role
CERT-InMeitYNational cybersecurity incident response, alerts and advisories.
I4CMinistry of Home AffairsCoordination of the national response to cybercrime.
National Cyber Crime Reporting PortalPart of the I4C reporting arrangementEnables the public to report cybercrime complaints.
State and Union Territory policeRespective State or Union Territory law enforcement authoritiesInvestigation and further legal action according to the applicable law.

Cybercrime helpline 1930

The national toll-free cybercrime helpline is 1930. It provides assistance in reporting cybercrime, especially where rapid action is needed after financial cyber fraud.

The National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal is available at cybercrime.gov.in. It accepts complaints concerning different types of cybercrime, with particular attention to crimes against women and children.

Under I4C, the Citizen Financial Cyber Fraud Reporting and Management System, introduced in 2021, supports rapid reporting and coordination with financial institutions to help prevent further movement of fraudulently transferred funds. The existence of this system does not mean that every reported loss can be recovered.

These arrangements remained part of India's operational national cybercrime response framework at the content cutoff of 17 November 2026, as described in the Ministry of Home Affairs statement dated 22 July 2026.

What a victim should do after a financial cyber fraud

  1. Contact the bank or payment service immediately: Use an independently verified official contact channel. Report the unauthorised transaction and request appropriate protective action on the affected account or payment facility.
  2. Call 1930 promptly: Report the suspected financial cyber fraud and provide accurate transaction details.
  3. Submit or complete the complaint through the national portal: Use cybercrime.gov.in to submit the complete fraud details, using the acknowledgement number received by SMS after reporting through 1930.
  4. Preserve evidence: Retain relevant messages, phone numbers, screenshots, transaction reference numbers, payment details and complaint acknowledgements.
  5. Secure affected accounts: Change compromised passwords using a trusted device, stop using suspicious applications and cooperate with the concerned bank and police.

Reporting quickly improves the opportunity for protective action, but filing a complaint does not guarantee recovery of money. The national portal receives complaints and supports coordination; the concerned State or Union Territory law enforcement agency handles investigation and subsequent legal action.

Application in Gujarat

A resident of Gujarat can use the same national helpline 1930 and the same reporting portal, cybercrime.gov.in. The complaint can then be handled through the relevant law enforcement arrangements, including Gujarat Police where the complaint falls within its jurisdiction.

The Ministry of Home Affairs also identified Ahmedabad among the locations covered by Joint Cyber Coordination Teams established to improve coordination among State and Union Territory law enforcement agencies in cases involving multiple jurisdictions. This illustrates the connection between national cybercrime coordination and Gujarat.

Connecting threats, precautions and responses

Malware is addressed through precautions such as genuine applications, updates and backups. Phishing is countered by independent verification and refusal to disclose passwords or OTPs. Strong passwords and 2FA reduce unauthorised account access. UPI fraud prevention depends on recognising that a UPI PIN authorises a debit and is not required merely to receive money. After suspected financial loss, the urgent response is to contact the financial institution, call 1930 and use the national cybercrime reporting portal. CERT-In performs a different function by providing national cybersecurity incident response and advisories.

Prelims focus

  • The Information Technology Act was enacted in 2000 as Act 21 of 2000.
  • Section 66C concerns identity theft; Section 66D concerns cheating by personation using digital means.
  • Section 70B concerns CERT-In, the national cyber incident response agency under MeitY.
  • I4C functions under the Ministry of Home Affairs.
  • 1930 is the national cybercrime helpline; the reporting portal is cybercrime.gov.in.
  • Trap: CERT-In is not the same institution as I4C, and a national portal complaint is not itself a guarantee of an FIR or refund.

pictures.alt: Cyber threats connect to protective actions, with a UPI PIN reminder, immediate financial fraud reporting routes and CERT-In’s statutory role.
pictures.caption: Cyber safety combines prevention, account protection, recovery and reporting.

title: The Information Technology Act, CERT-In and Reporting Cybercrime in India
